id=report-2.9  source=ssoc_report  ~tokens=166  meta={'page': 12, 'para': '2.9', 'section': 'Structure of SSOC'}
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SSOC 2024 Report — §Structure of SSOC
2.9 The use of educational categories to operationally define the four broad job levels does not imply that the ability to perform the tasks and duties of a given job can be acquired only through formal education. It can also be acquired through continuing education and training, on-the-job training and experience. In addition, the focus of SSOC is to classify jobs whose main tasks and duties are characterised by a high degree of similarity and not on whether a worker in a particular occupation is more or less qualified or proficient than another worker in the same occupation. Arrangement of the Classification Structure

==========================================================================================
id=report-2.10  source=ssoc_report  ~tokens=235  meta={'page': 12, 'para': '2.10', 'section': 'Structure of SSOC'}
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SSOC 2024 Report — §Structure of SSOC
2.10 The numerical codes of the SSOC 2024 are closely aligned with the ISCO-08 to facilitate comparison between the two classifications where possible. As such, the codes at the two-, three- and four-digit levels may not run consecutively if an ISCO code is not used in the SSOC. For instance, the SSOC does not contain the ISCO code 1113 ‘Traditional Chiefs and Heads of Village’. However, in some cases there may be insufficient vacant codes to accommodate new occupations in the local context. Some of the SSOC 2020 five-digit codes when dropped or subsumed under another occupational group due to redundancy or low counts of the occupation, may be reused for another occupation in SSOC 2024 so that the codes run consecutively and there are codes freed up to accommodate the new occupations. Hence, users need to refer to both the occupational codes and titles when comparing SSOC 2024 and SSOC 2020.

==========================================================================================
id=report-2.11  source=ssoc_report  ~tokens=326  meta={'page': 12, 'para': '2.11', 'section': 'Structure of SSOC'}
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SSOC 2024 Report — §Structure of SSOC
2.11 The SSOC 2024 comprises five levels of aggregation, namely the major group, sub-major group, minor group, unit group and occupation: Major Groups (one-digit or alphabetical codes) are the highest level of aggregation and represent very broad fields of work rather than specific types of work performed. There are 10 major groups, including nine numerical groups for various occupational groups, each identified by a corresponding one-digit from 1 to 9, and a Group X for occupations not elsewhere classified. Sub-major Groups (two-digit codes) are the sub-divisions of the major groups e.g. Science and Engineering Professionals (Sub-major Group 21) within the Major Group 2 ‘Professionals’. Minor Groups (three-digit codes) are the sub-divisions within the sub-major groups e.g. Engineering Professionals I (Minor Group 214) within the Sub-major Group 21 ‘Science and Engineering Professionals’. Unit Groups (four-digit codes) are sub-divisions of the minor groups. The classification of unit groups is finer and more detailed than that of the minor groups e.g. Civil Engineers (Unit Group 2142) within the Minor Group 214 ‘Engineering Professionals I’. Occupations (five-digit codes) are sub-divisions of the unit groups and the most detailed groupings in SSOC.

SSOC 2024 Report — §Structure of SSOC
2.13 A numerical or alphanumeric five-digit coding system is used to denote the different levels of classification. The numbering system is hierarchical in nature, showing from the highest level of aggregation (one-digit) to the most detailed level (five-digit). This allows users the flexibility to tabulate, analyse and publish data according to the level of detail required. An example of the different levels under Major Group 2 is shown below. ==========================================================================================
id=report-2.14  source=ssoc_report  ~tokens=182  meta={'page': 13, 'para': '2.14', 'section': 'Structure of SSOC'}
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SSOC 2024 Report — §Structure of SSOC
2.14 While the SSOC is a hierarchical system, all occupations in the same major group have the same broad job levels. The ordered arrangements of occupations in the sub-major, minor and unit groups within the same major group do not imply different complexity of the occupations. For instance, occupations in Major Group 2 are all associated with the same Broad Job Level 4 or possibly 3. It does not mean that Sub-major Group 21 ‘Science and Engineering Professionals’ has a higher broad job level and is more complex than Sub-major Group 22 ‘Health Professionals’. Similarly, Sub-major Group 22 is not of a higher significance or complexity than Unit Group 2655 ‘Actors’. Scheme of Coding

==========================================================================================
id=report-2.15  source=ssoc_report  ~tokens=197  meta={'page': 14, 'para': '2.15', 'section': 'Structure of SSOC'}
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SSOC 2024 Report — §Structure of SSOC
2.15 Generally, in cases where a given level of classification is not divided into groups or occupations at the next more detailed level of classification, the last digit of the code for the only group or occupation at the next detailed level would be ‘0’. This holds true for ‘0’ at the four- and five-digit levels. For instance, the Unit Group ‘Secretaries and Verbatim Reporters’ is coded as 4120 as the Minor Group ‘Secretaries and Verbatim Reporters’ (code 412) contains only one unit group. On the other hand, at the two- and three-digit levels, ‘0’ may be used to denote supervisory category instead. For instance, Sub-major Group ‘Clerical Supervisors’ (code 40) is not the only sub-major group in the Major Group 4 ‘Clerical Support Workers’.

==========================================================================================
id=report-2.16  source=ssoc_report  ~tokens=197  meta={'page': 14, 'para': '2.16', 'section': 'Structure of SSOC'}
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SSOC 2024 Report — §Structure of SSOC
2.16 At a given level of aggregation other than the one-digit level, the digit ‘9’ that appears in the last digit position at the respective level denotes residual occupations grouped at the respective level. These residual categories usually comprise a range of the less common types of occupational groups which are not significant enough to justify a separate code. They are classified in a separate category so that no occupation, however small or insignificant, is left out of the classification scheme. The description of such codes usually ends with the term ‘not elsewhere classified’ at the two-digit to four-digit levels and the abbreviation ‘n.e.c.’ at the five-digit level. Detailed Definitions, Alphabetical Index and Correspondence Tables

==========================================================================================
id=report-2.17  source=ssoc_report  ~tokens=239  meta={'page': 14, 'para': '2.17', 'section': 'Structure of SSOC'}
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SSOC 2024 Report — §Structure of SSOC
2.17 Detailed definitions are available for occupations (five-digit code) and unit groups (four-digit code). The definition of an occupation (five-digit code) includes a brief lead statement describing the key tasks and duties of the workers, to help users distinguish the different occupations. Unit group definition contains a brief lead statement describing the key tasks and duties of the workers and a more detailed listing of the tasks. Where the tasks are not common for an occupation, they are qualified with the word ‘may’ in the statements. For example, the occupational definition for training manager is: Occupation 12123 Training manager Training manager plans, directs and coordinates the training and development activities of the staff of an organisation. He/she may also design and develop new training modules and supervise all the activities related to the planning and delivery of these programmes.

==========================================================================================
id=report-2.18  source=ssoc_report  ~tokens=204  meta={'page': 14, 'para': '2.18', 'section': 'Structure of SSOC'}
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SSOC 2024 Report — §Structure of SSOC
2.18 The SSOC’s alphabetical index contains a wide variety of commonly used titles used to describe occupations. It enables users to link the alternative occupation titles, including Singapore Skills Framework (SFw) job roles, to the principal occupation titles used in the classification structure. It should be noted that the alphabetical index is not exhaustive. Jobs with titles that are ambiguous, or where a particular SFw job role can be mapped to several possible SSOC codes, are excluded from the listing (e.g. Designer in the SFw – Design, which can be coded under various SSOC depending on the type of design done). The alphabetical index is a useful tool to assign classification codes to responses to the questions in statistical and administrative data collections.

==========================================================================================
id=report-2.19  source=ssoc_report  ~tokens=134  meta={'page': 14, 'para': '2.19', 'section': 'Structure of SSOC'}
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SSOC 2024 Report — §Structure of SSOC
2.19 Two-way correspondence tables between SSOC 2024 and SSOC 2020, and SSOC 2024 and ISCO-08 are available at the most detailed level. Correspondence tables between SSOC 2024 and SSOC 2020 help users to link or backcast data that are in different versions of the SSOC due a change to the scope, creation of new codes or deletion of existing codes. Correspondence tables between SSOC 2024 and ISCO-08 also enable users to convert SSOC-based data into ISCO, facilitating international comparability.

==========================================================================================
id=report-2.20  source=ssoc_report  ~tokens=83  meta={'page': 15, 'para': '2.20', 'section': 'Structure of SSOC'}

SSOC 2024 Report — §Structure of SSOC

SSOC 2024 Report — §Classification Principles
3.1 The classification principles form the basis on which the SSOC 2024 is structured and applied. Basic Principles

==========================================================================================
id=report-3.2  source=ssoc_report  ~tokens=116  meta={'page': 15, 'para': '3.2', 'section': 'Classification Principles'}
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SSOC 2024 Report — §Classification Principles
3.2 The primary objective of the SSOC is to classify all the occupations of the civilian working population, but with provisions for the collective classification of those in the armed services and the foreign diplomatic personnel in occupations X3000 and X4000. It is not applicable to persons outside the labour force such as housewives, full-time students, retired persons and voluntary/non-salaried social workers.

==========================================================================================
id=report-3.3  source=ssoc_report  ~tokens=84  meta={'page': 15, 'para': '3.3', 'section': 'Classification Principles'}
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SSOC 2024 Report — §Classification Principles
3.3 Occupations are classified according to the type of work performed. Persons who perform the same principal tasks and duties are considered as doing the same type of work and classified under the same occupational group regardless of work experience, employment status and qualifications.

==========================================================================================
id=report-3.4  source=ssoc_report  ~tokens=79  meta={'page': 15, 'para': '3.4', 'section': 'Classification Principles'}
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SSOC 2024 Report — §Classification Principles
3.4 Broad job level provides a useful indication on where to classify a job. However, it should be emphasised that a job’s principal tasks and duties take priority over the broad job level in determining where to classify the job. Occupations with Multiple Tasks and Duties

==========================================================================================
id=report-3.5  source=ssoc_report  ~tokens=473  meta={'page': 15, 'para': '3.5', 'section': 'Classification Principles'}
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SSOC 2024 Report — §Classification Principles
3.5 Some occupations may involve a variety and range of tasks and duties that could fall under the specified scope of various occupations, and the principal tasks are not possible to be ascertained. In such cases, the following rules shall apply, in the order of precedence given below: (a) In cases where the tasks and duties performed require different broad job levels, the job should be classified according to those tasks and duties which require the highest job level (i.e. Broad Job Level 4 followed by Broad Job Level 3 and so on). For example, a job which requires driving a van and delivering goods should be classified in Unit Group 8322 ‘Car, Taxi, Van and Light Goods Vehicle Drivers’ (Broad Job Level 2) instead of Unit Group 9333 ‘Material and Freight Handling Workers’ (Broad Job Level 1). (b) In cases where the tasks and duties are associated with different stages of the process of producing and distributing goods and services, the tasks and duties related to the production stage should take priority over associated tasks and duties, such as those related to the sales, marketing and transportation of the same goods. For example, a worker who bakes bread and pastries and then sells them, should be classified as a baker and not a sales worker. (c) In cases where the tasks and duties are of the same broad job level and at similar production stage, then the fundamental predominance rule applies based on assumptions of the most amount of time spent on specific main tasks/duties. For example, a worker who cooks lunch and takes care of children in an after-school child care centre would likely spend more time attending to the needs of the children instead of cooking for them and would be classified as a child/after school care centre worker instead of a cook. Managing Directors, Chief Executives and General Managers

==========================================================================================
id=report-3.6  source=ssoc_report  ~tokens=200  meta={'page': 16, 'para': '3.6', 'section': 'Classification Principles'}
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SSOC 2024 Report — §Classification Principles
3.6 Managing directors, chief executives or general managers in Unit Group 1120 determine and formulate policies, plan, direct and coordinate the activities of their companies or organisations. They are generally assisted by at least two other managers, and operate within guidelines from their boards or councils. Those with similar job titles but whose job scopes do not fulfil the above criteria are classified in occupations corresponding to their job duties and scopes of work. Managers responsible for specialised functions within a specific geographic area are excluded from this unit group. For example, regional sales managers are classified in Unit Group 1221 ‘Sales and Business Development Managers’ instead. Managers and Size of Organisation

Workers classified in Sub-major Groups 12 ‘Administrative and Commercial Managers’ and 13 ‘Production and Specialised Services Managers’, may be employed in large hierarchical organisations or in relatively small organisations that provide specialist services to other organisations.

3.8 Information about the size of the organisation in which an individual manager is employed is not generally relevant to decisions about the most appropriate SSOC code. This is because SSOC Major Group 1 is organised according to functional specialisation and not according to the size of the organisation managed. To ascertain whether a job should be classified under SSOC Major Group 1, information on both the job title and the main tasks or duties performed should be obtained. The main tasks or duties would take priority in determining where to classify the job. Working Proprietors

3.12 Apprentices and trainees are classified according to the occupation they are training for, if they are employed in the capacity of apprentice or trainee.1 Apprentice carpenters and apprentice electricians, for example, are classified as carpenters and electricians. SSOC 2024 Report — §Comparison with SSOC 2020
4.1 The more significant changes in the SSOC 2024 compared to SSOC 2020 are summarised below: 1 Where students are undertaking work practice not as part of an employment arrangement (e.g. as an intern undergoing unpaid work attachment programmes), they are not classified according to economic activity status as employed, and their learning activity would therefore not normally be classified by occupation. As this situation may be fairly common in educational programmes for particular occupational groups, care should be taken to check their economic activity status when considering occupational titles such as “student teacher” or “pupil nurse” in statistical collections. • SSOC 2024 replaces the terms “skill specialisation” and “skill level” with “broad job specialisation” and “broad job level” respectively. • New occupations in Infocomm Technology, Green Economy and other sectors that are distinct from SSOC 2020 codes have been added. • New three-digit Minor Group ‘Social Services, Counselling and Related Professionals’ has been created to distinguish social services related professionals from social science researchers and religious professionals. • Some occupations across major groups and unit groups have been reclassified due to developments in main tasks/duties of occupations over time. • About 20 SSOC codes, mainly under Major Groups 7 and 8, have been removed or merged due to obsolete or low employment counts. • Improvements to alphabetical index, detailed definitions and occupational titles in classification structure have been incorporated.

Creation of New Three-digit Minor Group for Social Services, Counselling and Related Professionals

4.9 A new three-digit Minor Group 266 ‘Social Services, Counselling and Related Professionals’ has been created to separately group social services related professionals, which were previously classified in the same minor group as social science researchers and religious professionals. Reclassification of Occupations Across Major Groups and Unit Groups

==========================================================================================
id=report-4.10  source=ssoc_report  ~tokens=221  meta={'page': 20, 'para': '4.10', 'section': 'Comparison with SSOC 2020'}
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SSOC 2024 Report — §Comparison with SSOC 2020
4.10 Some occupations have been reclassified across unit groups, taking into consideration the main tasks and duties of these occupations in the context of Singapore and developments in recent years. For instance, ‘multimedia games designer’ and ‘interaction designer’ have been reclassified from Unit Group 2166 to Unit Group 2512 given that the nature of work is more related to information and communications technology (ICT). Another example is the reclassification of ‘Educarer’ from Major Group 5 to Major Group 3. This takes into account that other than just providing care and supervision, educarers also plan and conduct educational and play activities that are intended to promote the development of children below primary school-going age, in line with the tasks of preschool educators in Major Group 3. SSOC 2024 Report — §Comparison with SSOC 2020
4.11 SSOC codes that are obsolete or have low employment counts have been removed. This is to ensure that the SSOC remains relevant and allows for new codes to be created to meet users’ needs. About 20 obsolete five-digit codes, mostly in Major Groups 7 and 8, have been merged into approximately 16 five-digit codes. Improvements to Alphabetical Index

==========================================================================================
id=report-4.12  source=ssoc_report  ~tokens=272  meta={'page': 21, 'para': '4.12', 'section': 'Comparison with SSOC 2020'}
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SSOC 2024 Report — §Comparison with SSOC 2020
4.12 Some 1,000 new alphabetical index entries have been added to facilitate easier coding. For comprehensiveness and ease of identifying occupational titles without the need to cross check between multiple documents, SSOC occupational titles have been added to the alphabetical index. They are labelled “Principal Title” to distinguish them from the alternative titles in the alphabetical index. An additional of some 270 new job titles have been added in the index by including constituent job titles from main occupational titles to facilitate the use of the index for coding. For example, SSOC 13302 ‘Software and applications manager’ will have “Software development manager” and “Application development manager” included in the alphabetical index as shown in the below table. SSOC 2024 SSOC 2024 Alphabetical Index Description Category 13302 Software and applications manager Principal Title 13302 Software development manager Alternative Title 13302 Application development manager Alternative Title Improvements to Detailed Definitions

SSOC 2024 Report — §Comparison with SSOC 2020
4.14 To improve stylistic coherence across the titles in classification structure and detailed definitions, stylistic edits have been implemented.

==========================================================================================
id=report-4.15  source=ssoc_report  ~tokens=200  meta={'page': 21, 'para': '4.15', 'section': 'Comparison with SSOC 2020'}
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SSOC 2024 Report — §Comparison with SSOC 2020
4.15 Where multiple occupations are mentioned in the five-digit occupational title, a “/” would be used for consistency and better distinction of the different occupations. Instances of “including” and “e.g.” in the main occupational titles will be removed, with these additional titles shifted to the illustrative examples in the detailed definitions for the occupation and/or added to the alphabetical index. Titles for residual codes from the sub-major group (two-digit) to occupation (five-digit) have also been aligned in the usage of terms “Other”, “Not elsewhere classified” or “n.e.c.”. The detailed definitions for the residual codes at the unit group (four-digit) and occupation (five-digit) have also been standardised. 5 Linking SSOC with SFw2

==========================================================================================
id=report-5.1  source=ssoc_report  ~tokens=117  meta={'page': 22, 'para': '5.1', 'section': 'Linking SSOC with SFw2'}
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SSOC 2024 Report — §Linking SSOC with SFw2
5.1 To facilitate analysis and comparison between SFw related information and SSOC, the SFw job roles have been mapped to relevant SSOC codes in the alphabetical index. New SSOC codes have been created if necessary, and changes to the scope and titles of existing SSOC codes have been made to improve the linkage between SSOC and SFw. The alphabetical index is updated half-yearly to take into account the refresh of the SFw.

==========================================================================================
id=report-5.2  source=ssoc_report  ~tokens=130  meta={'page': 22, 'para': '5.2', 'section': 'Linking SSOC with SFw2'}
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SSOC 2024 Report — §Linking SSOC with SFw2
5.2 Nonetheless, it should be noted that SSOC and SFw are not directly comparable due to differences in coverage, construct and purpose. SSOC is a statistical classification that is adapted from ISCO to ensure international comparability and covers all occupations whereas SFw provides information on sectors, new and changing job roles, as well as in-demand and emerging skills required for the job roles. 6 How to Determine the Appropriate Occupational Code for an Occupation

==========================================================================================
id=report-6.1  source=ssoc_report  ~tokens=339  meta={'page': 22, 'para': '6.1', 'section': 'How to Determine the Appropriate Occupational Code for an Occupation'}
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SSOC 2024 Report — §How to Determine the Appropriate Occupational Code for an Occupation
6.1 There are two ways to find an appropriate SSOC code in SSOC 2024: (a) Refer to the alphabetical index or use the SingStat SSOC Search to look for the job title by which the occupation is known, and select the most appropriate SSOC code by referring to the detailed definition. Consideration should be given to possible synonyms and abbreviations of the words in the job title; or (b) Refer to the classification structure to classify the job broadly, either at the sub-major, minor group or unit group level before narrowing down to the most appropriate five-digit code at the occupational level. The choice of SSOC code should be confirmed by referring to the detailed definition. 2 The Skills Framework (SFw) is an integral component of the Singapore’s Industry Transformation Maps. It aims to create a common skills language for individuals, employers training providers and tripartite partners which facilitates skills recognition and support the design of training programmes for skills and career development, enhance business competitiveness and support employment and employability. As at end-December 2023, there were 35 sectoral SFws and over 1,790 job roles covering more than two-thirds of the workforce. Part II: Classification Structure of SSOC 2024
